newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen opening firmer, watching CPI.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen opening firmer, watching CPI.

text.p: Wall Street is seen opening higher Thursday, taking its cue from the U.S. Consumer Price Index, which is expected to confirm the growing belief that inflation is not threatening the economy.
April CPI, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, is forecast to rise 0.1 percent for the second straight month. Excluding food and energy, "core" CPI is seen up 0.2 percent, also for the second month in a row.
"The market will be directed by economic news this morning," said Peter Cardillo, Westfalia Investments analyst.
Other economic data due this morning will also guide the market, offering insight into whether Federal Reserve policy makers will opt to raise interest rates when they meet next Tuesday.
Initial jobless claims for the week ended May 10, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are forecast at 340,000, versus 347,000 in the previous week.

April industrial production and capacity utilization are due at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT. Industrial output is forecast up 0.2 percent versus a rise of 0.9 percent in March. Capacity utilization is seen flat at 84.1 percent.
"If the economy shows a big hike in capacity utilization, that raises the question of inflation, which could dampen any enthusiasm from the PPI and CPI," Cardillo said.
The dollar, which was trading weaker against both the mark and the yen, was also seen boosting the stock market.

"The weakness in the dollar indicates that currency traders expect no action on the interest rate front, which should be positive for the market," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
But analysts said the market could lose energy later in the day, and pointed to the bond market, which was trading off.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average closed down 153.41 points, or 0.76 percent, at 20,056.31.
In London the FTSE 100 was down 29.8 points at 4657.1. U.S. stocks in London were little changed.
The dollar was weaker against the yen in Tokyo, trading at 116.10/20, and was at 1.6906/09 against the mark in Europe.
The U.S. Treasury 30-year bond was off 10/32 to yield 6.91. The Standard & Poors 500 futures index was up 0.20 to 840.15.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said Paine Webber strategist Edward Kerschner, who has been bullish on stocks, has turned neutral and now says the market is more likely move 10 percent lower before rising 10 percent.
The New York Times's Market Place column said Response USA issued an unusual sort of preferred security last summer in order to secure a loan.
